questions.problem:
Let $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -1 & k\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ where $k$ is a constant such that $k\ne -3.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $det(A)\ne 0$

II. $Ax=0$ has no solutions

III. The lines $x+3y=-1$ and $-x+ky=1$  intersect at exactly one point.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -1 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot k-(-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =k+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $k+3\ne 0$ if $k\ne -3.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the unique solution to  $Ax=0$ is the trivial one (zero).

- Statement III is true by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Finally, only statements I and III are true.

questions.problem:
Find the determinant of the matrix 
$Q=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the $4$th column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(Q) & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+4}|\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| & =-5\cdot (2\cdot 1\cdot 3)=-30.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
det(Q)=-30.
$$

questions.problem:
The domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+(1+t)\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\,k$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \bbox[5pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}.
$$

What is the missing expression? You may assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the domain of $f$, we need the intersection of the domains of the individual components.

- The domain of the 1st component $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 2nd component $1+t$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 3rd component $\operatorname{cot}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4})$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ except for the values of $t$ for which

$$
t-\frac{\pi }{4}=\pi n\,⟹\,t=\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

Therefore, the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Determine the number of pivot columns of the matrix $D,$ given by

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 & 7 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to convert $D$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 & 7 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 & 7 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $D$ has $3$ pivots, and therefore the number of pivot columns is $3.$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 9\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y-(-5)}{0}=\frac{z-1}{9}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+5}{0}=\frac{z-1}{9},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{y+5}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=-5:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}t \\ -5 \\ 1+9t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y+5}{0}$ part and instead write $y=-5,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{1}=\frac{z-1}{9},\,y=-5
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y={(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x}))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})+x\cdot ((2x)\cdot (-\frac{2}{(2x)^{2}})) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})-1 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-{(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1) \\  & =-{(2x)}^{-x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
An eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}]$ 
corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda =3k-2$ is $[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 5k\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 5k\end{aligned}] & =(3k-2)[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 5k\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -30+35k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6(3k-2) \\ (5k)(3k-2)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -30+35k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-18k+12 \\ 15{k}^{2}-10k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6=-18k+12 \\ -30+35k=15{k}^{2}-10k\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
-6=-18k+12\,⟹\,k=1.
$$

Now, substituting $k=1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-30+35k & =15{k}^{2}-10k \\ -30+35\cdot 1 & =15\cdot {1}^{2}-10\cdot 1 \\ 5 & =5,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=1.$

What is the name of the polyhedron shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The solid is a **rectangular pyramid** since it has a rectangular base and the other $4$ triangular faces meet at a single point.   

Also, notice that:

- The solid is not a cube since not all of its faces are squares.

- The solid is not a triangular prism because it does not have two triangular bases connected by parallel line segments.

- The solid is not a triangular pyramid since its base is not triangular.

- The solid is not a heptagonal pyramid since its base is not a heptagon.
